 The UofA and the city of Fayetteville recognized Indigenous Peoples’ Day on Oct. 12 with a proclamation ceremony at the Union Multicultural Center. University officials and tribal representatives discussed the importance of tribal sovereignty, cultural identity and Native American representation in higher education. The event also highlighted campus resources for Indigenous students and efforts to preserve Native languages, histories and traditions.

 The city of Fayetteville collaborated with the University of Arkansas to officially recognize Indigenous Peoples’ Day citywide on Oct. 12. Tribal representatives shared indigenous peoples’ importance in the field of education and Mayor Molly Rawn read an Indigenous Peoples’ Day proclamation. 
 Columbus Day, a U.S. federal holiday since 1937, is celebrated annually on the second Monday in October. Indigenous Peoples’ Day has become an alternative holiday that recognizes the Native American groups who inhabited North America before European settlement.  
 Indrajeet Chaubey, the UA provost and executive vice chancellor for academic affairs, said the university is working toward building better relationships with surrounding tribes. 
 “Recognizing the separate government, histories and identities of each tribal nation is fundamental to building meaningful relationships,” Chaubey said. “These relationships become stronger when we come together and we are made to listen, learn and deepen our understanding.” 
 The university has recognized Indigenous Peoples’ Day for 22 years, starting in 2004. Registered student organizations such as the Native American Student Association and the Native American Student Services Office have celebrated this holiday through annual speaker events and occasional ceremonies at the Trail of Tears marker on Martin Luther King Boulevard. 
 The university is located directly along the Cherokee removal route. In front of Old Main, a statue titled “ Courage to Lead ” recognizes the UofA and Trail of Tears connection, representing the Native American history that resonates within the region. 
 Ash Dotolo, a sophomore political science and international studies major, is a citizen of the Cherokee, Shawnee and Delaware nations. 
 “The University of Arkansas holds a unique position where many of its indigenous students feel deeply disconnected from their tribal groups,” Dotolo said. “The university has an opportunity to invest in these students not only as students growing into their professional careers, but as students growing into their tribal identities.” 
 Dotolo is an intern at the UA Native American Student Services . The office focuses on helping indigenous students by promoting cultural growth and removing any barriers they may face through Native American courses, tribal connection and other student success advising. It also offers guidance on applying for tribal scholarships. 
 “I’ve learned not only more about my cultural connection, but my cultural history,” Dotolo said. “Growing up, my only tribal connection was my grandmother, who I didn’t come to know personally until around three years ago.” 
 Dotolo said she found a new appreciation for the mutually beneficial relationship between people and nature after reading "Braiding Sweetgrass" by Robin Wall Kimmerer. 
 Braiding Sweetgrass is a collection of essays composed by Robin Wall Kimmerer discussing indigenous history, the connection between humans and nature and damages over the centuries. This is done through a combination of scientific research and Kimmerer's personal experience. 
 “[Kimmerer] discusses the land as one of our greatest teachers,” Dotolo said. “This idea of mutually beneficial reciprocation is integral to indigenous thought, practices and many of our cultures.” 
 This is Fayetteville’s 17th official proclamation recognizing Indigenous Peoples’ Day since the tradition began in 2009. 
 Understanding the meaning of tribal sovereignty is important when acknowledging modern Native American nations, said Aaron Emberton, executive director for the Cherokee Nation ’s Education Services Department. 
 “Tribal sovereignty is the inherited pride of the Native nations to govern themselves, to preserve and teach their cultures, and to shape the paths their citizens walk,” Emberton said. “When we talk about sovereignty and education, we’re talking about the ability to determine what customs are learned, how they learn it and how their identity and history is honored throughout that process.” 
 Emberton said that for generations, Native citizens have been taught what offenses were done to their tribes rather than how they can start healing and rebuilding. 
 “Federal policy sought to erase languages, traditions, community ties and inflicted violence on some of our most innocent,” Emberton said. “Native nations have the authority, as well as the responsibility, to reclaim education as a tool for not only cultural survival, but try to strengthen and grow.” 
 When education respects sovereignty, students will see themselves in their learning, Emberton said. 
 “Tribal connections with higher education institutions ensures that Native students see themselves reflected in their stories and know their values,” Emberton said. “When students see themselves in the school they attend, they succeed. The tribal sovereignty doesn’t just impact students positively. Higher education benefits as well.” 
 Emberton said one of the goals of the Cherokee Nation is growth of the Cherokee language. 
 “It means preserving cultural touchstones, values and stories,” Emberton said. “When institutions like the University of Arkansas offer tribal language courses, it benefits tribal citizens and noncitizens alike.” 
 The UofA currently offers Elementary Cherokee I and II courses. 
 The Multicultural Center, where the proclamation occurred, displays 193 flags in the International Connections Lounge, all from member states of the United Nations, said Jeremy Battjes, the UA vice chancellor of student affairs. 
 “We will soon be adding the flags of the sovereign tribal nations,” Battjes said. 
 To close the ceremony, Fayetteville Mayor Molly Rawn declared Oct. 12 as Indigenous Peoples’ Day after reading the proclamation aloud. 
 According to the UA Native American Student Services, the Quapaw, Osage, Caddo and Tunica-Biloxi tribes are the original peoples of NWA. The Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek, and Seminole Nations were forcibly removed through the Fayetteville area during the Indian Removal Act of 1830.
